TROUBLE IS EXPECTED
SHERIFF AND HIS DEPUTIES GO FOR NEGROES.
Mobile Officers Well Armed and May Kill a Few Would-be Assassins Who Threatened to Slay White Man.
Advertiser Bureau,
Mobile, Aug. 26.

Sheriff Powers today received a telegram from a deputy at Oak Grove, Ala., reading as follows:

"Send two deputies to Bradley on Citronelle train this afternoon. Riot brewing there. Will join them here."

The telegram was signed by W. S. Brewster, a reliable deputy, located at Oak Grove, a lumber manufacturing place, about fifteen miles north of Mobile. Bradley is a flag station on the Mobile and Ohio just north of Oak Grove, where a mill is running, owned and operated by the Vinegar Bend Lumber Company.

Hardly had the sheriff received the message when T. N. Mashburn, manager of the Bradley mill, appeared in the office and stated that he was looking for trouble with the negroes at his mill. He said he had discharged some of the negroes yesterday evening and they had threatened to kill him. When he left Bradley this morning he was informed that the negroes had armed themselves with Winchesters and pistols and had declared they would kill him as soon as he returned there. This news also reached Deputy Brewster at Oak Grove, hence his message to the sheriff.

Sheriff Powers with three deputies left on the Citronelle train at 3:30 for Bradley. They went above the station a short distance, got off the train and went back to the station. Here they were informed the negroes had gone to Beaver-Meadow to a picnic. Sheriff Powers decided, having warrants for the negroes, to go to that station with a view of apprehending the would-be assassins. He and his posse are well armed and in event they come upon the negroes there will be something doing.

NEGROES THREATEN MANAGER OF PLANT
(By Associated Press.)
MOBILE, ALA., August 26.—Sheriff Powers and four deputies left late to-day for Bradley, on the Mobile and Ohio Railroad, where is located the plant of the Bradley Lumber Company. Negroes had trouble with Manager Mashburn, and, arming themselves, have threatened to kill him and burn the mill property. There is no telegraphic communication with the place, so no details are at hand.

FOR THE LEGISLATURE.

Montgomery Democrats Nominate Chas. A. Johnston.

(Special to The Times-Dispatch.)
CHRISTIANSBURG, VA., Aug. 26. There was a large turn out of Democrats to-day to attend a mass-meeting here held for the purpose of reorganizing the party in this county. The meeting was thoroughly harmonious and enthusiastic. An executive committee was elected, which re-elected Colonel Sidney Sheltman as county chairman.

The legislative convention, composed of delegates from Radford and this county, was convened on the adjournment of the committee. The work of this body was also short, as Mr. Charles A. Johnston received the nomination by acclamation. It is conceded that the convention acted wisely and has selected the strongest man in the county to contest with the Republicans. The hope of the Republicans that the late primary had engendered bad blood among the Democrats was entirely dissipated by to-day's proceedings, and they realize that a united party confronts them. The Democrats are better united than they have been for years.

The Radford delegates after the senatorial nomination withdrew, and the county convention nominated Captain H. D. Wade for county clerk and W. J. Halt as his deputy. The feature of the convention was the earnest and eloquent speeches made by Judge Phlegar in nominating Captain Wade, and latter in response to repeated calls on him.

CROWN PRINCESS NOW
LEADER OF FASHIONS

(Special Cable to The Times-Dispatch and New York Herald.)
(Copyright, by the New York Herald Co.)
BERLIN, Aug. 26.—The Crown Princess of Germany has just introduced a new fashion here, which although not quite unknown, is likely to find great favor among the "smart set." While walking the Crown Princess almost invariably makes use of a dainty and rather long walking stick, with a golden top and a silken bow tied to it.

The Crown Princess' example has been followed lately by a good many society ladies. Her Royal Highness has a large collection of sticks, so as to be able to select one to suit any costume she may be wearing.

One very handsome mauve colored stick is finished off at the top with a flat crystal button bearing the initials of Her Imperial Highness in rubles.

The Crown Princess, by reason of her youth and refined taste, is rapidly becoming a leader of fashion in Berlin society.

Advertiser Bureau.
Mobile. Aug. 27.

Sheriff Powers and Deputies Cherry, Tom Powers and Will McCarron returned this morning at 7:30 from an all night and afternoon's chase after a gang of negroes from Bradley, on the Mobile and Ohio Railroad, north of here. As noted in The Advertiser of this date, the Sheriff yesterday received notice that a number of negroes at Bradley, a sawmill station, had armed themselves and were lying in wait for T. N. Mashburn, a woods foreman for the Bradley mill, owned and operated by the Vinegar Bend Lumber Company.

With the deputies named, Sheriff Powers left here at 3:30 on the Citronelle accommodation train, went north of Bradley a short distance, dropped from the train and made his way back to Bradley, only to find the negroes had gone to Beaver Meadow, still further north of here, but in this county. In the meantime Deputy Sheriff W. S. Brewster had joined the posse. The party arrived at Beaver Meadow early in the night. Here they had better success than at Bradley. They came across three of the negroes, who opened fire on the officers. The fire was promptly returned and Deputy Sheriff Cherry is positive he brought down one of the negroes, though he could not be found, owing to the location and hour of the night. It is thought by the posse that the negro, even if only wounded, was carried away by his comrades.
At 1 o'clock this morning Deputies Cherrv. Tom Powers and McCarron went to Bradley and made a search of every negro shack on the hill. Only one negro was found, but he was not wanted. The posse, after boarding the southbound mail this morning, made two happy catches. One was Babe Thomas, a negro who has been wanted here on a warrant charging assault with intent to murder, and who has been out of the State for quite a period. He was discovered on the blind baggage and promptly taken in charge. Just a little further down the line the deputies discovered another negro on the blind baggage, and he was also captured. He proved to be George Richardson, an escaped convict from the Vinegar Bend Lumber Company's camp. While the posse had a hard round of it on their trip and were completely fagged out when they reached here, they are satisfied in that they scattered the belligerent negroes from Bradley and landed two criminals in the county jail.

Notwithstanding the Sheriff's posse returned to the city, Deputy Brewster and a number of white men from Bradley and Beaver Meadow continued the search this morning, having better results than the Sheriff. One of the negroes, Boston Moore, was apprehended

OFFICERS CAPTURE
ONE RINGLEADER
NEGRO WAS MEMBER OF GANG THAT CREATED DISTURBANCE AT BRADLEY, ALA., FRIDAY AND FRIDAY NIGHT.
Mobile, August 27.—Deputy Sheriff Brewster arrived here tonight from Oak Grove, Ala., having in custody Boston Moore, one of the ringleaders in the trouble which occurred at Bradley, Ala., a mill town three miles above there, Friday night.

Sheriff Powers and three deputies went to the scene of the trouble Friday night and returned here this morning after a search of some hours, being unable to capture any of the negroes engaged in the trouble. Deputy Cherry reports that on Friday the four ringleaders went into the store of the Bradley Lumber company armed with shotguns. One negro, Charles Denton, cursed one of the white men, thereupon Newton Mashburn, team boss of the mill, remonstrated with the negro, who went out and returned with three others. They stood in the store door and cocked their guns, threatening to kill the white men. They were driven to a hill and opened fire on the men at the store, who returned the fire.

No one was hurt among the whites, and it is not known if any of the negroes were hit, although a shirt with blood on it was found in the swamp.

THE QUARANTINE SITUATION.
Meridian Quarantined Against on Account of Lax Methods.
Macon's Position Upheld by the Action of Meridian's Citizens Protesting Against Lax Qnarantine.
Macon, like the balance of the State, on Saturday, when a case of fever was reported at Lumberton, put a quarantine on all towns on the Northeastern below Meridian and guards were appointed to meet the trains to see that our town and county did not become a place of refuge for the infected section. There is hardly a plantation of any size in this section thus is not represented in the cow counties by three of four negroes, and it is natural, as soon as the panic struck them, rush back to their old homes, their friends and relatives.

Meridian, unfortunately, is the clearing house for the whole of north and east Mississippi. On Sunday evening last a number of negroes got off the train with tickets and health certificates from Meridian, but upon being questioned acknowledged that they had come from points on the Northeastern road which had been quarantined against and stated that they had "purchased their health certificates from a man at the depot." Meridian's lax method was further demonstrated by testimony from reputable parties that drummers had stated openly that they had come directly out of New Orleans into Meridian without being questioned. In view of these facts the board of aldermen met and decided to quarantine against Meridian until that city could be notified that her health officers were being imposed on by anxious fugitive and that they were jeopardizing their neighboring counties, but Meridian became upish and notified Macon through its Dement(ed) yellow journal, The Sta that she would run her quarantine suit herself and no little upstart like Macon should complain. Almost Race War. There came very nearly being a race war at Rockport this county, last Sunday. It seems that a negro and a white man got into a row on the streets about 11 o'clock Saturday night and another negro and white man took it up and each emptied, his revolver. Things quieted down until some time Sunday morning when it was learned about thirty negroes had congregated out side of town and defied arrest. Several white men armed themselves and went out to arrest the negroes and several shots were fired but no one seriously injured. The Police Judge called the Sheriff Sunday about noon and asked
that he come or send some one to Rockport at once to make arrests of the offending parties. The Sheriff's reply was, as we are informed, that he would come if a writ was placed in his hands and not otherwise. A negro by the name of Render came to town Monday and made affidavit and had a writ issued for fifteen white men, some of them, the best citizens of Rockport. A representative of the white men came to Hartford yesterday and told the Sheriff that each one for whom a writ had been issued would come to Hartford and surrender. We are informed that some of the parties whose names appear in the affidavit and writ were not even in or near Rockport at the time. It is said that a rope was left at a negro's house Monday night together with a note which notified him to leave at once or he would be hanged. The negro we are told had recently said: "He had served a term in the 'pen' for killing one white son of a b-h and he would soon get another son of a b-h." The full particulars will be given in these columns after the trial.

CLASH AT ROCKPORT.
Between About Thirty Negroes And Fifteen to Twenty- ty Whites.
A clash between the negroes and whites at Rockport began last Saturday night and assumed serious proportions before the engaging parties were quieted. If is reported that the trouble grew out of a trivial matter, some dispute arising between one of the colored fellows and a white man about a lunch, perhaps five cents worth of cheese, and they engaged in abuse one of the other, during which the colored fellow called the white man a d n s o b which the white fellow resented others joined in and a general fight occurred. Volley after volley were fired from the ever ready pistols but no one was seriously hurt. Finally about midnight all the belligerents acquitted the scene and all became quiet.

The fight was renewed the next day (Sunday) when a report reached Rockport that several negroes had congregated and armed themselves and were on their way to town. The whites did not wait for them to arrive but about fifteen or twenty armed themselves with pistols, rifles and shot-guns and sallied forth to meet the negroes, a crowd of whom they found at Pet Render's. They opened fire on the dark skins and in a short while put them to flight.

One of the negroes who was in these fights came to Hartford Monday and had a warrant issued for fifteen of the whites who are alleged to have been engaged in the difficulty. The warrant, which charges them with banding together to disturb or injure other persons, upon conviction for which one to five years in the penitentiary being the penalty, was placed in the hands of Deputy Sheriff Chester Keown who went to Rockport Wednesday to execute it. After spending the whole day executing the warrant and making arrangements to bring those arrested to Hartford, he was directed by County Attorney W. H. Barnes to turn the warrant over to the Rockport Police Court where the examining trial will be had.

Negro Boys Convicted of Disorderly Conduct Flogged By Parents. Taylorsville, Ky., Aug. 18.—Judge G. B. Shindler, of the Taylorsville Police Court, set a good example by having some young negroes whipped for disorderly conduct. Seven negro boys, ranging in age from twelve to eighteen years, were arraigned before the Judge when he entered a fine to each of $3, with the proviso that if their parents would give them a good whipping they could be released from jail. A large crowd congregated to see the public whipping. The boys were taken out, one by one, by their parents, and, under the supervision of Marshal Jewell, were subject to a severe castigation. Owingsville, Ky., Aug. 18.—[Special.] —The Republican Committee of Bath county met here and fixed September 5 as a date to hold another meeting, when a time will be named to hold a convention to nominate candidates for Bath county offices. A full ticket will be put out, but it is not believed that a candidate for Representative will be placed in the Jackson Will Entertain Convention. Campton, Ky., Aug 18.—The Republican committee of this, the Thirty-fourth senatorial district, met at Cannel City, Morgan county, and called a general convention to be held at Jackson September 1 for the purpose of nominating a candidate for State Senator. Indictment Charges Willful Murder. Harlan, Ky., Aug. 18.—The grand jury of the present term of the Harlan Circuit Court has returned an indictment against B. M. Cox, charging him with the willful murder of Carlo Hall two months ago. MINISTER COMBS LEAVES FOR GUATEMALA TO-DAY.
Leslie Combs, United States Minister to Guatemala, arrived in the city yesterday afternoon from Lexington, where he had been spending several weeks during his leave of absence from his post of duty. He was accompanied by Mrs. Combs, and they were the guests of Capt. Sam H. Stone and family at their home, 913 Third street, last night. Mr. and Mrs. Combs will leave this morning for California, where they will spend some time in traveling over that country before sailing for Guatemala. Mr. Combs is due at Guatemala September 1. He will take a steamer from San Francisco to a port on the western coast of Guatemala, which is only about seventy-five miles from Guatemala City. During their absence from Guatemala Mr. and Mrs. Combs have visited their daughter in Germany as well as friends and relatives at their old home in Lexington.

Didn't Know It Was Hot.

Theodore Knies, employed at the Baltimore dairy lunch on Market street, severely burned his right hand last night at 9 o'clock. One of the employees had been using the gas stove, and the burner was red hot. He turned out the gas, and Knies, not knowing the stove had been in use, attempted to lift the heated burner out. It was necessary for a physicist to dress the injury.
